samples.ask: Tell how a mango seed grows into a mango tree, in five or six sentences.
samples.answer: First, a mango seed falls into the soil. When the monsoon rain comes, the seed soaks up water and opens. Next, a tiny root grows down and a green shoot grows up. After a few months, the shoot becomes a small plant with leaves. Over many years, it grows into a tall tree. Finally, flowers appear and turn into mangoes.
key_points: five or six stages in the right order

samples.ask: Imagine you are a raindrop. Tell your journey from a cloud to the sea in five or six sentences.

After that, the stream carried me into a wide river. For many days, I floated past villages and fields. At last, the river poured me into the salty sea.
key_points: five or six sentences in a sensible order

samples.ask: Describe a busy vegetable market on a Sunday morning. Write four or five sentences and use at least two senses.
samples.answer: The vegetable market is noisy and crowded on Sunday morning. Sellers sit behind tall piles of red tomatoes, purple brinjals and green chillies. They shout their prices over the honking of scooters. The air smells of fresh coriander and wet earth. Shoppers squeeze past each other with heavy cloth bags.
key_points: describes the market with chosen details
uses at least two senses
does not turn into a list of events

samples.ask: Write the opening paragraph of a story that describes the old empty house at the end of Lane 4. Use three senses and one comparison, so the reader wants to find out more.
samples.answer: At the end of Lane 4 stands a house that nobody visits. Its windows are cracked like broken spectacles, and creepers have wrapped the gate in green ropes. When the wind blows, the door creaks open and slams shut again. The air near the steps smells of damp wood and old dust. Some evenings, a faint yellow light flickers in the attic, even though no one has lived there for years.
key_points: describes the house with chosen details
uses three senses
uses one comparison
ends with a detail that makes the reader want to read on

samples.ask: Describe Captain Raghav, the strict but fair captain of the school kabaddi team, so a reader can picture him. Include his looks, how he moves and speaks, and one comparison.
samples.answer: Captain Raghav is tall and broad, with short hair that stands up like a brush. He walks onto the field with long, firm steps, and the whole team goes quiet. His voice is deep and loud, but he never shouts at anyone who has tried their best. When a player is hurt, he kneels beside them and speaks gently. His eyes are sharp, so he notices every mistake and every good move.
key_points: describes his looks
describes how he moves and speaks
shows he is strict but fair
uses one comparison

samples.ask: Describe Diwali night as seen from the rooftop of a building. Use three senses and one comparison so the reader feels they are there.
samples.answer: From our rooftop, the whole city twinkles with lamps. Strings of lights hang from every balcony like glowing necklaces. Rockets whistle into the dark sky and burst into showers of gold and green. The smell of smoke mixes with the sweet smell of jalebis from the flat below. I can feel the warm air on my face as I hold my little sparkler tightly.
key_points: describes the scene with chosen details
uses three senses
uses one comparison
keeps to describing the moment

samples.ask: Describe a cave that no one has entered for a hundred years, and make it feel mysterious. Then write one sentence saying which detail you think will make the reader want to read on.
samples.answer: The mouth of the cave is hidden behind a curtain of thick roots. Inside, the air is cold and still, and every footstep echoes like a whisper coming back. Water drips from the roof and gathers in black pools that shine like glass. On the far wall, someone has carved strange shapes that look like eyes. Far away in the dark, something rattles softly and then stops. I think the carved eyes will make the reader want to read on, because they make us wonder who made them.
key_points: builds a mysterious mood with chosen details
uses more than one sense and a comparison
names one detail and explains why it hooks the reader

samples.ask: Describe a robot that works in a library, a character you have made up. Show its personality through how it looks and what it does.
samples.answer: Pustak is a short, round robot with a shiny copper body that is covered in tiny dents. Its two blue eyes glow softly, like lamps on a foggy night. It rolls silently between the shelves so that it never disturbs a reader. When a child cannot reach a book, Pustak stretches its long arm and hands it over with a little bow. If anyone speaks loudly, it raises one metal finger to the small speaker on its face and beeps, very politely, "Shhh."
key_points: describes an imagined character with chosen details
shows personality through actions
uses a comparison
every part of the task is there

samples.ask: Describe a night market as a small mouse would see it from the ground, so that everything seems huge.
samples.answer: From under the fruit stall, the night market is a forest of giant legs. Sandals as big as boats thump past my nose, and I have to dodge them quickly. Above me, lanterns hang like burning moons. The smell of roasted corn is so strong that my whiskers twitch. A peanut shell falls beside me with a crash like a falling rock. The roar of voices never stops, and I press myself against a cool, damp crate until the crowd moves on.
key_points: describes from the mouse's point of view throughout
makes ordinary things seem huge
uses several senses and comparisons
builds a clear mood

samples.ask: Write a new ending for the story. In your ending, the crow cannot find any pebbles. Begin with: The crow looked around, but there were no pebbles anywhere.
samples.answer: The crow looked around, but there were no pebbles anywhere. Then he saw a long, hollow straw lying near the tree. He picked it up in his beak and pushed it into the pot. He sucked hard, and the cool water came up the straw. The clever crow drank until he was full.
key_points: keeps the crow, the pot and the little water from the story
has no pebbles, and the crow solves the problem another way
finishes the story clearly

samples.ask: Write a new ending in which a girl from the village helps the crow. Begin with: Just then, a girl called Sita came to the tree.
samples.answer: Just then, a girl called Sita came to the tree with a jug of water. She saw the tired crow hopping around the pot. Gently, she poured fresh water into the pot until it was full. The crow drank happily. After that, he visited Sita every morning, and she always left water for him.
key_points: keeps the thirsty crow and the pot
Sita helps the crow
the ending finishes the story

samples.ask: Write a new beginning for the story that tells why the crow was so thirsty. Begin with: It was the hottest day of the summer.
samples.answer: It was the hottest day of the summer. The sun burned in the sky, and the ground cracked in the heat. The crow had flown all morning to find food for his babies. Now his throat was dry and sore, and he could not see a single drop of water anywhere.
key_points: explains why the crow is thirsty
leads into the story as it is
uses chosen words for the heat

samples.ask: Write a different ending for the story, starting from the moment the kite gets stuck. Do not use Mr Joshi in your ending.
samples.answer: Meera sat down on the terrace and felt like crying. Then Kabir had an idea. He tied a small stone to a piece of string and threw it gently over the branch. When it came down on the other side, he pulled slowly, and the branch bent low. Meera reached up and freed her kite. It was a little torn, so they mended it with tape and flew it together until sunset.
key_points: starts when the kite is stuck
does not use Mr Joshi
Meera and Kabir act as they do in the story
the problem is solved

samples.ask: Write a new beginning for the story that shows how Meera got her new red kite.
samples.answer: The day before Makar Sankranti, Meera went to the market with Aaji. Hundreds of kites hung from the stalls like coloured birds. Meera had saved her pocket money for weeks, but most kites cost too much. At the last stall, she found a bright red kite with a long tail. Aaji added the last ten rupees, and Meera carried it home as carefully as an egg.
key_points: shows how Meera got the kite
leads into the story the next morning
uses chosen details

samples.ask: Write a different ending in which the kite string snaps and the kite floats away.
samples.answer: Meera tugged one more time, and suddenly the string snapped. The red kite floated free and drifted over the rooftops. Meera and Kabir watched it go, feeling sad. A few minutes later, a little girl on a nearby terrace caught it and waved happily. Meera smiled and waved back. Then Kabir gave her his own kite, and they flew it together until sunset.
key_points: the string snaps and the kite floats away
Meera and Kabir react as the story's characters would
the ending closes the story

samples.ask: Write a new ending for the story, starting from the moment Arjun finds the monkey. Make it fit Arjun, who is quiet but notices things.
samples.answer: Arjun did not shout or run at the monkey. Instead, he sat down quietly on a rock and watched it. He noticed that the monkey kept looking at a baby monkey hiding in a tree. Slowly, Arjun broke off a piece of thepla and placed it on the ground. The monkey took it to the baby and left the tiffin box behind. When Arjun told the class, his friends Zoya and Dev were amazed, and they shared their lunch with him.
key_points: starts when Arjun finds the monkey
Arjun stays quiet and notices a detail
fits what has already happened
the problem is solved clearly

samples.ask: Write a new beginning for the story that starts on the bus to the fort. Show the reader that Arjun is quiet but notices things.
samples.answer: The bus to Sinhagad Fort was full of noise. Everyone was singing and shouting, but Arjun sat by the window and said nothing. He was watching the hills. While the others played games, he spotted a hawk circling over the road and a family of monkeys sitting on a wall. He held his bag tightly on his lap, because his mother had packed his favourite theplas.
key_points: is set on the bus before the story begins
shows Arjun is quiet
shows Arjun notices things
leads into the rest of the story

samples.ask: Write a different ending in which the trail of crumbs leads Arjun to a surprise of your own. It must still fit what has already happened.
samples.answer: Arjun followed the crumbs quietly behind the wall. There, under a tree, sat a little stray dog with his tiffin box between its paws. The dog was very thin, and it wagged its tail weakly when it saw him. Arjun felt sorry for it, so he let it finish the theplas. When he told the class, Zoya and Dev shared their lunch with him, and the guide promised to take the dog to a shelter.
key_points: the crumbs lead to a new surprise
keeps Arjun quiet and kind
fits the trip and the missing tiffin
the ending closes the story

samples.ask: Write a different ending in which Gopal wishes for gold. Show what happens to him, so the ending still fits the story's message.
samples.answer: Gopal's eyes shone. "I wish for a room full of gold," he said. The old woman nodded and disappeared. The next morning, Gopal's hut was full of gold, but he was too busy counting it to make any pots. Soon the families had nothing to cook in, and the children stopped visiting. Gopal sat alone among his gold coins, feeling lonelier than ever. At last he picked up some clay, sat at his wheel and began to make a pot. As it turned, he smiled for the first time in weeks.
key_points: Gopal wishes for gold
shows what the wish costs him and the village
the ending still shows that helping people matters
fits Gopal and the old woman

samples.ask: Write a new ending told by the old woman, saying what she thought when Gopal made his wish.
samples.answer: I have granted many wishes, and most people ask for gold. When Gopal's eyes shone, I was sure he would ask for it too. Then I saw him look at his wheel and the pots drying in the sun. I watched him think of the children and the families. When he wished that his hands would always help people, my heart felt warm. I walked away into the dusk smiling, because I knew he had found what he was looking for.
key_points: told by the old woman in the first person
shows what she thought before and after the wish
keeps the same wish and events
fits the story's message

samples.ask: Write a new beginning that sets the story in a busy city today instead of a village long ago. Then write one sentence saying how this changes the story.
samples.answer: In a crowded street in Pune, between a phone shop and a tea stall, there was a tiny pottery shop. Gopal sat at his wheel every day while scooters roared past and buses honked. His pots were strong, but most people walked past to buy plastic buckets from the big stores. "If only I were rich like the shop owners on Main Road," he sighed. Setting the story in a city today makes Gopal's wish harder, because people there buy plastic instead of clay pots.
key_points: moves the setting to a city today
keeps Gopal a potter who wants to be rich
explains in one sentence how the change affects the story

Read about the peafowl. Fill in the table with short notes about its tail and its food.

You are making a poster called Why the Monsoon Matters. Make short notes for it in the table.

samples.ask: Make four short notes about the history of Sinhagad Fort. Then use your notes to write a short paragraph for a class display.
samples.answer: Notes: once called Kondhana; walls on cliff edges; 1670, Tanaji climbed cliffs at night; renamed Sinhagad, Lion's Fort. Paragraph: Sinhagad Fort was once called Kondhana. Its walls were built along the edges of the cliffs, so it was hard to attack. In 1670, the brave warrior Tanaji Malusare and his soldiers climbed the cliffs at night and captured it. Sadly, Tanaji died in the battle, so the fort was renamed Sinhagad, which means Lion's Fort.
key_points: four short notes on the history, not on visiting
notes are key words, not sentences
the paragraph uses every note in a sensible order

samples.ask: Make short notes on what visitors can see and do at the top of Sinhagad. Then use them to write a short guide for younger children.
samples.answer: Notes: old gates; water tanks cut in rock; Tanaji memorial; pithla bhakri and buttermilk at stalls. Guide: When you reach the top of Sinhagad, look for the old gates first. Next, find the water tanks that were cut into the rock long ago. Then visit the memorial to the brave warrior Tanaji. Before you walk back down, try some hot pithla bhakri and a glass of cool buttermilk from the stalls.
key_points: notes cover what to see and what to eat
notes are short
the guide uses the notes and suits younger children

samples.ask: Make short notes on when and how to visit Sinhagad. Then use them to write a short paragraph for the school newsletter about planning a family trip.
samples.answer: Notes: 30 km south-west of Pune; walk up path or go by road; best October to February; path slippery in monsoon. Paragraph: Sinhagad Fort is about thirty kilometres south-west of Pune, so it makes a good day trip. Families can walk up the winding path or travel most of the way by road. The best time to go is from October to February, when it is cool. Try not to go in the monsoon, because the path can be very slippery.
key_points: notes on where it is, how to get there and when to go
notes are short
the paragraph is written from the notes for families

options: Luckily, his friend Farhan lent him a spare one.
Anil woke up late on the morning of the cricket match.
With Farhan's bat, Anil scored twenty runs and his team won.
Because he was in a hurry, he forgot to pack his bat.
When he reached the ground, he saw that it was missing.
answer: Anil woke up late on the morning of the cricket match.
Because he was in a hurry, he forgot to pack his bat.
When he reached the ground, he saw that it was missing.

With Farhan's bat, Anil scored twenty runs and his team won.

samples.ask: These sentences tell why the class plants died, but they are mixed up. Number them in the right order.
options: While she was away, nobody remembered to water the plants.
In April, our class planted sunflower seeds in pots by the window.
As a result, when she came back, the leaves were brown and dry.
Every morning, Neha watered them, so they grew quickly.
Then Neha went to visit her grandmother in Nashik for two weeks.
answer: In April, our class planted sunflower seeds in pots by the window.
Every morning, Neha watered them, so they grew quickly.
Then Neha went to visit her grandmother in Nashik for two weeks.
While she was away, nobody remembered to water the plants.
As a result, when she came back, the leaves were brown and dry.

samples.ask: These steps for making poha are mixed up. Number them in the right order.
options: When the oil is hot, add mustard seeds, onion and curry leaves.
Finally, sprinkle coriander on top and serve it hot with lemon.
First, wash the flattened rice and leave it to soften.
Once the onion is soft, stir in the rice with salt and turmeric.
While it softens, heat a little oil in a pan.
answer: First, wash the flattened rice and leave it to soften.
While it softens, heat a little oil in a pan.
When the oil is hot, add mustard seeds, onion and curry leaves.
Once the onion is soft, stir in the rice with salt and turmeric.
Finally, sprinkle coriander on top and serve it hot with lemon.

samples.ask: Use these notes to write a paragraph about the school sports day. Put the ideas in order and link them with at least three different linking words.
samples.text: Notes: march around the field; younger classes' races; kabaddi final 4A v 4B, very close; prizes; everyone tidies up
samples.answer: Our school sports day began early in the morning with a march around the field. After the march, the younger classes ran their races while we cheered from the stands. Next came the event everyone was waiting for, the kabaddi final between Class 4A and Class 4B. It was so close that nobody knew who would win until the last raid. When the match was over, the principal gave out the prizes. Finally, everyone helped to tidy the field before going home.
key_points: uses every note in the right order
links ideas with at least three different linking words
each sentence follows on from the last

samples.ask: Use these notes to explain how to plant a tulsi sapling. Write a paragraph, not a list, and link each step to the one before.
samples.text: Notes: fill pot with soil; make hole; put sapling in, press soil; water; sunny spot (needs light)
samples.answer: Planting a tulsi sapling is easy if you follow the steps in order. First, fill a clay pot with soil, leaving a little space at the top. Then make a small hole in the middle with your finger. After that, place the sapling in the hole and press the soil gently around it so that it stands up straight. Once it is planted, water it well. Finally, put the pot in a sunny spot, because tulsi needs plenty of light to grow.
key_points: follows the steps in the order of the notes
uses at least three different linking words
is a paragraph, not a list

samples.ask: Use these notes to write a paragraph explaining why the school started a No Plastic Day. Show how each idea leads to the next.
samples.text: Notes: plastic thrown in canal; monsoon, drains blocked; road by gate floods; children miss school; class writes to principal; No Plastic Day every Friday
samples.answer: Last year, a lot of plastic bags and wrappers were thrown into the canal behind our school. When the monsoon came, the plastic blocked the drains. As a result, the water had nowhere to go, so the road near the school gate flooded. Many children could not get to school for two days. Because of this, our class wrote a letter to the principal. She agreed with us, and now every Friday is No Plastic Day.
key_points: explains the causes and results in order
uses linking words for cause and result, such as because and so
each idea leads to the next

samples.ask: Use these notes to write a paragraph explaining what happened to the village well. Use linking words for time, cause and contrast, such as because, as a result and however.
samples.text: Notes: well gave water for years; village grew, more pumps; well dried up; women walk to river; villagers build small walls to trap rain; well fills again
samples.answer: For many years, the well in Wadgaon gave sweet water to every family. However, when the village grew, people began to dig new wells and use pumps all day. Because so much water was taken out, the old well slowly became dry. As a result, the women had to walk two kilometres to the river every morning. The villagers decided to act. They built small walls across the stream to trap the monsoon rain, so the water soaked back into the ground. The next year, the old well filled up again.
key_points: explains causes and results in a logical order
uses links for time, cause and contrast
each idea builds on the one before
the ending shows the result of the villagers' action

samples.ask: These ideas are jumbled. Write them as one paragraph in a logical order. Then add one sentence explaining why you chose that order.
samples.text: Ideas: the poster wins first prize; Sana sees Ishan eating alone; Ishan helps make the poster because he is good at drawing; Sana invites him to sit with her friends; by Friday he smiles every morning
samples.answer: On Monday, Sana noticed that the new boy, Ishan, was eating lunch alone. She invited him to sit with her friends. Because Ishan was good at drawing, he helped them make a poster for the science fair. As a result, their poster won first prize, and Ishan became part of the group. However, the best part was that by Friday he was smiling every morning. I put the ideas in this order because each one happened because of the one before it.
key_points: puts the ideas in a logical order
links them with words for time, cause and contrast
explains why the order works

samples.ask: Write a paragraph explaining how a small seed can become a tall mango tree. Make clear how each stage leads to the next, and use at least one link for contrast.
samples.answer: A mango tree begins as a single seed inside the stone of a fruit. When the stone falls into damp soil, the seed soaks up water and begins to swell. Soon a root pushes down into the ground, so the seedling can drink. After that, a shoot grows upwards towards the light. Young mango plants grow slowly at first. However, once their roots are deep, they grow quickly. After about five years, the tree is tall enough to flower, and then the flowers turn into new mangoes.
key_points: explains each stage in order
shows how each stage leads to the next
uses at least one link for contrast
uses links for time and cause

samples.ask: Finish the scene. Write four more lines for Isha and Nikhil. Put one stage direction in brackets.

Scene: The school canteen.
ISHA: Nikhil, have you seen my tiffin box?
NIKHIL: (shaking his head) No. Where did you leave it?
samples.answer:
ISHA: (looking under the table) I put it right here before the bell.
NIKHIL: Look, there is a blue box on the window sill. Is that yours?
ISHA: Yes! I must have left it there when I opened the window.
NIKHIL: Quick, let us eat before the bell rings again.
key_points: four new lines, each with the speaker's name and a colon
at least one stage direction in brackets
the lines follow on from the first two

samples.ask: Finish the scene. Write four more lines for Grandpa and Aman. Put one stage direction in brackets.
samples.text:
Scene: A park on a rainy evening.
GRANDPA: (looking at the sky) Aman, those clouds are very dark.
AMAN: Is it going to rain?
GRANDPA: Any minute now. We should start walking home.
samples.answer:
AMAN: But Grandpa, we have no umbrella!
GRANDPA: (laughing) Then we will get wet together, like when I was a boy.
AMAN: Will Mum be cross?
GRANDPA: Not if we bring her hot bhajiyas on the way home.
key_points: four new lines with names and colons
at least one stage direction in brackets
the lines follow on from the start

samples.ask: Finish the scene. Write four more lines for Mrs Rao and Kiran. Put one stage direction in brackets.
samples.text:
Scene: A bus stop in the monsoon.
MRS RAO: Kiran, why are you standing in the rain?
KIRAN: (sadly) I missed the school bus, and I do not know how to get home.
samples.answer:
MRS RAO: Do not worry, Kiran. I can call your father from my phone.
KIRAN: (smiling) Thank you, Mrs Rao. His number is in my diary.
MRS RAO: Good. You can wait under my umbrella until he comes.
KIRAN: That is very kind of you.
key_points: four new lines with names and colons
at least one stage direction in brackets
the lines solve Kiran's problem

YUSUF: It is shivering. It must be lost.
SARA: (kneeling down) Come here, little one. Do not be scared.
YUSUF: It has a red collar. Maybe there is a name on it.
SARA: It says Bruno, and there is a phone number too.
YUSUF: Let us take it to the guard so he can call the owner.
key_points: six lines for Sara and Yusuf, each with a name and a colon
two stage directions in brackets
a listener can follow what happens

BOY: (searching his pockets) Oh no! I have left my money at home.
SELLER: Where do you live?
BOY: Just in the next building, near the temple.
SELLER: (handing him the bag) Take the bananas. You can pay me tomorrow.
BOY: Thank you, Uncle! I will bring it first thing in the morning.

two stage directions in brackets
the problem is clear and solved through talk

samples.ask: Write a short scene of six lines in which two sisters both want the last piece of barfi at Diwali. Use two stage directions in brackets.

RIYA: (grabbing the plate) The last barfi is mine!
ANU: That is not fair. You have already had three.
RIYA: But I helped Mum make them.
ANU: (folding her arms) So did I. I stirred the milk for ages.
RIYA: All right. Let us cut it in half.
ANU: Good idea. Happy Diwali, Riya!
key_points: six lines with names and colons
two stage directions in brackets
a listener can follow the argument and how it ends

samples.ask: Write a short scene for three friends who are practising for the school play when one of them forgets her lines. Add a scene heading and at least two stage directions.
samples.answer:
Scene: The school hall, after lunch.
MEHA: (holding a script) Let us start again from the beginning.
ROHIT: I am the king, so I go first. Who dares to enter my palace?
ZOYA: (opening her mouth, then stopping) I am... I am...
MEHA: You are the brave farmer, Zoya. Remember?
ZOYA: (covering her face) I have forgotten everything!
ROHIT: Do not worry. Say it with me slowly.
ZOYA: I am the brave farmer, and I have come to ask for rain.
key_points: a scene heading
each line has a name and a colon, with no speech marks
at least two stage directions in brackets, in the present tense
a listener can follow the problem and how it is solved

samples.ask: Write a short scene in which a girl and her grandfather get lost in a crowded market during the Ganesh festival. Add a scene heading and at least two stage directions.
samples.answer:
Scene: A crowded street during the Ganesh festival.
ASHA: (holding his hand tightly) Ajoba, I cannot see our street any more.
AJOBA: Neither can I. There are so many people.
ASHA: The drums are so loud!
AJOBA: (looking around) We came past a sweet shop with a blue sign.
ASHA: (pointing) There it is, next to the big pandal!
AJOBA: Clever girl. Our lane is just behind it.
ASHA: Can we buy some modaks first?
key_points: a scene heading
names and colons on every line
at least two stage directions in brackets
the problem and its solution come out through talk

samples.ask: Write a short scene inside an auto-rickshaw. A driver, a mother and her son are hurrying to catch a train. Add a scene heading and at least two stage directions.
samples.answer:
Scene: An auto-rickshaw on a busy road in Pune.
MOTHER: (checking her watch) Our train leaves in fifteen minutes!
DRIVER: Do not worry, madam. I know a short cut.
SON: (bouncing in his seat) Faster, faster!
MOTHER: Sit still, Neel, or you will fall.
DRIVER: (turning into a lane) Here we are, the back gate of the station.
MOTHER: Thank you so much! Come on, Neel, run!
key_points: a scene heading
three characters, each line with a name and a colon
at least two stage directions in brackets
a listener can follow the hurry and the ending

samples.ask: Turn this story paragraph into a playscript scene. Use a scene heading, the characters' lines and stage directions instead of a narrator.
samples.text: Manish ran up the steps, shouting that he had won the drawing competition. His grandmother put down her book and asked what he had drawn. When he said it was the old banyan tree with her sitting under it, her eyes filled with tears, and she hugged him tightly.
samples.answer:
Scene: The front steps of a house. Evening.
MANISH: (rushing up the steps) Grandma, guess what? I won the drawing competition!
GRANDMA: (putting down her book) Oh, Manish! What did you draw?
MANISH: Our old banyan tree, with you sitting under it.
GRANDMA: (wiping her eyes) Me? Under our tree?
MANISH: Yes. The judge said it was full of love.
GRANDMA: (hugging him tightly) Then it is the best drawing in the world.
MANISH: (grinning) Can we hang it in the hall, next to the clock?
GRANDMA: Of course we can.

no narration; directions in brackets in the present tense

samples.ask: Write a scene on a spaceship where two astronauts disagree about which button to press. Use stage directions to show feelings the characters do not say aloud.
samples.answer:
Scene: The control room of a spaceship far from Earth.
KAVERI: (calmly) The red button will turn on the back-up engine.
ARYAN: (wiping sweat from his forehead) No, it is the green one. I read the manual.
KAVERI: (her hand shaking slightly) I am the captain. We press red.
ARYAN: (staring at the warning light) And if you are wrong?
KAVERI: (taking a deep breath) Then we try green. Ready?
ARYAN: (nodding slowly) Ready.
(Kaveri presses the red button. The lights flicker, then glow bright.)
ARYAN: (laughing with relief) You were right!
key_points: names, colons and a scene heading
directions show fear or relief that the lines do not say
the disagreement and its ending are clear through talk

samples.ask: Write a scene for three characters at a village well long ago, when a stranger arrives. Add a list of characters, a scene heading and stage directions.
samples.answer:
Characters: LALITA, a girl; GOVIND, her brother; STRANGER, an old traveller.
Scene: A village well at sunrise, long ago.
LALITA: (lowering the bucket) The rope is getting old, Govind.
GOVIND: Father will make a new one after the harvest.
(A tired STRANGER walks slowly towards the well, leaning on a stick.)
STRANGER: Children, may I have a little water? I have walked all night.
LALITA: (looking at Govind, then filling a cup) Of course. Please sit.
STRANGER: (drinking) You are kind. In return, let me fix your rope.
GOVIND: (surprised) You know how to make rope?
STRANGER: (smiling) I have made rope for kings.
key_points: a list of characters and a scene heading
names and colons on every line, no speech marks
stage directions show movement and feeling
the lines show each character's personality
